title: Rupert Cole joins Armstrong's band and loses at blackjack
summary: Cole came from Don Redman's band, sight-read Armstrong's hard book as lead alto, won at blackjack on his first night and never again.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: I'll continue by asking you to flesh out portraits of musicians who may have not been in the spotlight. Somebody like Rupert Cole.

Oh, Rupert Cole, alto player, clarinetist. He was a very good musician. He joined the band, I don't know exactly when, what the date was, he had some pretty stiff music to put in front of him when he joined the band.

With Louis, yeah. Louis Armstrong. And he sat right down and read it off just like he'd been playing it all the time. No big deal, you know, with him. He played the show and everything. Beautiful. Stepped right in and played it.
And he was first alto, too, wasn't he?
Yeah. He was lead alto. And naturally, we become good chums anyway; I mean, I knew him anyway.

Always the boys had a little blackjack game going -- in our spare moments, which wasn't many. Well, anyway, Rupert Cole comes in the band the first night, and he got kind of lucky there. He won quite a few dollars the first night. Boy, I looked at him with admiration. "Oh boy, a gambler too." Man, he had everything going for him. So he was
enthused. He come into a fine band, a nice bunch of guys -- and lucky, win the money, too. So he was happy. I can't say how happy he was, but he was very happy.

And the next day, well, naturally the games keep on, you know; we play every day. And he didn't do so well the next day. The fellows kind of got in his money. Taken all of his little winnings and a little bit out of his pocket. Then it wasn't so nice. But he just stuck with it. He stayed in them days, and he was trying to get lucky again. Which he never did get lucky again. I never seen him win any more money til I had left the band. I don't know if he ever won any more. I stayed there... Let me see. I think I worked with Cole a few months anyway; I don't know how long we worked together until I left the band. And I never hear him win no more.
But he was a beautiful saxophone player, believe me. Good clarinettist.
Well, he had come from Redman, I think.

He came from Don Redman's band, yeah. He was lead saxophone with Don Redman. And he praised Don to the highest, you know. Well, Don was a great musician; there's no getting around that. Anybody that knew Don would know he was a great musician. And one thing he liked about Don, he said Don never told him anything about leading a

section. He just left him on his own, and he could lead the section any way he wanted to. And I thought that was a compliment in itself. He didn't have to tell him what he wanted. He thought very highly of Don for that, you know.
Cole was a nice person, but things happen in a band, you know... Well, things happen anywhere. And things just don't always go down just the way that they should go.
